quote: Provided that no scheme under clause (b) or (c) estimated to cost more than a crore of rupees shall be carried out by the Board except with the approval of the State Government.
provision: Section 15(2)(b)-(c) and proviso; Section 14 also reviewed
clause: Section 15(2) proviso (inserted by Act 6 of 1966); Section 14(1) and 14(4)(i)
comments: Score: 0 (no formal role for the city corporation (the ULG) in BWSSB's plan-making can be established). Under the BWSSB Act, 1964, BWSSB's main sectoral plans are its water supply and sewerage 'schemes'. Section 15(2)(b) and (c) give the Board the duty of 'preparing and carrying out' these schemes. The only approval required is from the State Government, for schemes costing more than Rs 1 crore (Section 15(2) proviso). The Act gives the city corporation no approval, concurrence or consultation role in preparing them. I agree with the Step 2 answer. The only possible link is Section 14, which does not meet the methodology's tests: (a) it is a Consultative Committee that the State Government sets up; (b) the State Government consults bodies representing interests, including the Municipal Corporation, only 'as the State Government thinks fit', and that consultation is about appointing members, not about plans; (c) the Committee only 'advise[s] the Board on major questions of policy and major schemes' (Section 14(4)(i)). So the corporation's involvement is indirect, decided by the State Government, and not a duty on BWSSB to consult the ULG on its plans. It is not even a 'may consult' provision directed at the Board. Section 38(2), which requires consultation with the Corporation Commissioner before closing a public hydrant, is operational, not plan-making. Scale: the methodology runs from 0 to 10 but the maximum here is 5. Because the score is 0, rescaling makes no difference. Gaps a reviewer should check: (1) the Karnataka Town and Country Planning Act is not in the Citation Sheet, so I could not check whether it requires sectoral plans to be coordinated with ULGs; (2) the Act text is a FAOLEX copy of uncertain date, so later amendments (for example, any reference to the Greater Bengaluru Authority or city corporations) may be missing; (3) BWSSB-22 and BWSSB-23 (JICA reports) describe coordination between BWSSB and BBMP but are not legal provisions.

quote: (a) The Sectoral Mobility Investment Program shall be aligned with the goals of the Comprehensive Mobility Plan; (b) The Sectoral Mobility Investment Program shall be prepared in consultation with the Authority;
chapter: Chapter VI – Sectoral and City Mobility Investment Program and Annual Implementation Plan (also Chapter V, Section 21(2) first proviso)
comments:
I propose a score of 0 because nothing in the Citation Sheet requires BMRCL to consult the ULG, or get its approval or concurrence, when preparing its sectoral plans. No source sets out such a role for the ULG. BMRCL is a Government company (a GoI–GoK joint venture, BMRCL-01). It was not set up by a parastatal Act, so no Act lays down its planning procedure.

I checked the Step 2 answer against the BMLTA Act (BMRCL-35), and it holds. BMRCL's principal sectoral plan, the Sectoral Mobility Investment Program, 'shall be prepared in consultation with the Authority' (Section 24(b)). Under Section 21(2), first proviso, other authorities 'shall necessarily consult the Authority'. In both cases 'the Authority' is BMLTA, a state transport authority, not the ULG. Section 20(1) does require consultation with 'Urban Local Bodies', but only for BMLTA's own mobility policies, such as parking and TOD. It does not apply to BMRCL's plans. Section 19 gives BMLTA, not the ULG, the power to approve projects.

One point needs a human check. The Greater Bengaluru Governance Act (BMRCL-34) names BMRCL in Section 14(4). It lets the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) integrate and supervise BMRCL's activities through 'directions … which shall be binding', and it says public authorities 'shall cooperate'. Under Section 15(1), the GBA 'shall be responsible to make master plan and mobility plans'. Under Section 15(5), the GBA 'may' assign the planning of major infrastructure to agencies, which are then 'bound to assist'. These are general coordination and direction powers. They are not a step in BMRCL's own plan-making that requires the GBA's consultation or concurrence, so they don't meet the 'shall consult'/concurrence test.

It is also unclear whether the GBA counts as the ULG. It is an apex statutory authority over the city corporations, not an elected municipal body. If a reviewer treats the GBA as the ULG and reads Section 14(4) as a coordination mandate covering BMRCL's planning, the score could change. Under the 10-point rubric that would be 10, which on this question's 5-point maximum would likely be 5.

The other sources don't change the result. The Metro Rail Policy 2017 (BMRCL-18) is advisory only. The parts of the T&CP Act (BMRCL-31) in the sheet deal with Master Plans by Planning Authorities, not metro agency plans. A score of 0 is the same on either scale.
